children.title: I. INTRODUCTION
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/I. INTRODUCTION
children.summary: This document is the first page of a survey paper titled "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey." It introduces the concept of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a solution to challenges like hallucination in Large Language Models (LLMs). The abstract outlines the paper's scope, which includes reviewing RAG paradigms (Naive, Advanced, Modular), frameworks, and evaluation methods. The introduction further details the rapid development of RAG technology and its integration into LLMs.

children.title: II. OVERVIEW OF RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/II. OVERVIEW OF RAG

children.title: A. Naive RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/II. OVERVIEW OF RAG/A. Naive RAG
children.summary: This page presents a technology tree of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) research, visualizing the evolution of methods from 2020 to 2024 across pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference stages. The text introduces the scope of RAG within Large Language Models (LLMs), outlines the paper's structure, and begins an overview of RAG paradigms including Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG.

children.title: B. Advanced RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/II. OVERVIEW OF RAG/B. Advanced RAG
children.summary: This page details the architecture and process of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), illustrated by a flowchart in Figure 2 that outlines the steps of indexing, retrieval, and generation. The text describes how Naive RAG functions through these three phases—converting documents into vector chunks, retrieving relevant context based on user queries, and generating answers using a Large Language Model (LLM). It also discusses challenges such as hallucination and redundancy, and introduces Advanced RAG strategies to improve performance.

children.title: C. Modular RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/II. OVERVIEW OF RAG/C. Modular RAG
children.summary: This page presents Figure 3, which visually compares three paradigms of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG. The text below the figure elaborates on pre-retrieval and post-retrieval processes, highlighting optimization strategies like query rewriting and reranking. It also details the Modular RAG architecture, emphasizing its flexibility through specialized components such as search modules and memory pools.

children.title: D. RAG vs Fine-tuning
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/II. OVERVIEW OF RAG/D. RAG vs Fine-tuning
children.summary: The section 'D. RAG vs Fine-tuning' compares Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Fine-tuning (FT) as optimization methods for Large Language Models (LLMs). It describes RAG as a method that leverages external knowledge sources, offering real-time updates and interpretability but with higher latency. In contrast, FT involves retraining the model to internalize knowledge, allowing for deep customization of behavior and style but requiring significant computational resources. The text notes that while unsupervised fine-tuning shows some improvement, RAG consistently outperforms it in handling new knowledge. The section concludes by stating that RAG and FT are not mutually exclusive and can complement each other.

children.title: III. RETRIEVAL
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL

children.title: A. Retrieval Source
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/A. Retrieval Source
children.summary: This section, titled 'A. Retrieval Source', discusses the types of data sources used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems to enhance Large Language Models (LLMs). It outlines the evolution from text as the primary source to include semi-structured data like PDFs and structured data such as Knowledge Graphs (KG). Additionally, it highlights a growing trend of utilizing content generated by LLMs themselves for retrieval and enhancement purposes.

children.title: SUMMARY OF RAG METHODS
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/A. Retrieval Source/SUMMARY OF RAG METHODS
children.summary: The page features Figure 4, a chart comparing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) with other model optimization methods based on the axes of 'External Knowledge Required' and 'Model Adaptation Required'. The figure illustrates that Prompt Engineering requires low external knowledge and adaptation, while Fine-tuning requires high adaptation. The text below discusses various data sources for retrieval systems, including unstructured data (e.g., Wikipedia, HotpotQA), semi-structured data (e.g., PDFs, tables via TableGPT), and structured data like knowledge graphs (e.g., G-Retriever). It also covers LLM-generated content and retrieval granularity.

children.title: B. Indexing Optimization
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/B. Indexing Optimization
children.summary: The section 'B. Indexing Optimization' discusses strategies for processing and segmenting documents into embeddings for storage in a vector database. It details three main approaches: Chunking Strategy (splitting text into fixed or recursive chunks, mentioning methods like Small2Big), Metadata Attachments (enriching chunks with page numbers, file names, or artificial metadata like hypothetical questions via Reverse HyDE), and Structural Index (establishing hierarchical structures like parent-child relationships or Knowledge Graphs to improve retrieval consistency and efficiency).

children.title: C. Query Optimization
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/C. Query Optimization
children.summary: The section 'Query Optimization' addresses the challenges of Naive RAG, such as imprecise queries and language ambiguity. It outlines several strategies to improve retrieval effectiveness: Query Expansion (enriching a single query with more context), Multi-Query (executing multiple expanded queries in parallel), Sub-Query (decomposing complex questions into simpler sub-questions), and Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) (validating expanded queries via an LLM to reduce hallucinations).

children.title: D. Embedding
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/D. Embedding
children.summary: The section discusses the role of embedding models in RAG systems, which calculate similarity between question and document chunks. It highlights prominent models like AnglE, Voyage, and BGE that benefit from multi-task instruction tuning. The text also mentions evaluation benchmarks such as Hugging Face's MTEB leaderboard (covering 8 tasks and 58 datasets) and C-MTEB for Chinese capability. Finally, it introduces 'Mix/hybrid Retrieval' as a method combining sparse and dense embedding approaches to capture different relevance features.

children.title: E. Adapter
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/III. RETRIEVAL/E. Adapter
children.summary: The section titled 'E. Adapter' discusses the use of external adapters to address challenges in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), such as limited computational resources or API integration constraints. It describes several approaches including UPRISE, which trains a lightweight prompt retriever; AAR (Augmentation-Adapted Retriever), a universal adapter for multiple downstream tasks; PRCA, a pluggable reward-driven contextual adapter; BGM, which uses a bridge Seq2Seq model between the retriever and LLM; and PKG, which employs advanced strategies like repetition.

children.title: IV. GENERATION
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/IV. GENERATION

children.title: A. Context Curation
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/IV. GENERATION/A. Context Curation
children.summary: The section 'A. Context Curation' discusses methods to process retrieved information before it is fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to avoid issues like the 'Lost in the middle' problem. It details two main approaches: 1) Reranking, which reorders document chunks based on relevance using metrics or models like BERT and GPT; and 2) Context Selection/Compression, which reduces context length by removing unimportant tokens or summarizing content using techniques like contrastive learning or small language models (SLMs).

children.title: B. LLM Fine-tuning
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/IV. GENERATION/B. LLM Fine-tuning
children.summary: This section discusses targeted fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve performance in specific domains or data formats. It highlights benefits such as incorporating additional knowledge, adapting to structured data (e.g., via the SANTA framework), and aligning outputs with human or retriever preferences through reinforcement learning. The text also covers distilling powerful proprietary models into smaller ones and coordinating fine-tuning between retrievers and generators using methods like RA-DIT.

children.title: V. AUGMENTATION PROCESS IN RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/V. AUGMENTATION PROCESS IN RAG

children.title: A. Iterative Retrieval
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/V. AUGMENTATION PROCESS IN RAG/A. Iterative Retrieval
children.summary: The section titled 'A. Iterative Retrieval' introduces a process where the knowledge base is repeatedly searched based on an initial query and previously generated text to provide more comprehensive knowledge.

children.title: B. Recursive Retrieval
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/V. AUGMENTATION PROCESS IN RAG/B. Recursive Retrieval
children.summary: The section 'B. Recursive Retrieval' describes a process used in information retrieval and NLP to improve search depth and relevance by iteratively refining queries based on previous results. It highlights methods like IRCoT, which uses chain-of-thought for guidance, and ToC, which creates clarification trees to optimize ambiguous queries. The text also notes that recursive retrieval is often combined with multi-hop retrieval techniques.

children.title: C. Adaptive Retrieval
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/V. AUGMENTATION PROCESS IN RAG/C. Adaptive Retrieval
children.summary: This section discusses adaptive retrieval methods, which enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to actively determine the optimal timing and content for retrieval. It highlights Flare and Self-RAG as examples of this approach. The text also contextualizes these methods within a broader trend of LLMs employing active judgment, similar to model agents like AutoGPT, Toolformer, and Graph-Toolformer. Additionally, it mentions WebGPT's use of reinforcement learning to train GPT-3 for autonomous search engine usage.

children.title: VI. TASK AND EVALUATION
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VI. TASK AND EVALUATION

children.title: A. Downstream Task
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VI. TASK AND EVALUATION/A. Downstream Task
children.summary: The section 'A. Downstream Task' outlines the primary applications of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models. It identifies Question Answering (QA) as the core task, covering various formats like single-hop/multi-hop QA and domain-specific scenarios. Additionally, it notes that RAG is expanding into other tasks such as Information Extraction (IE), dialogue generation, and code search. The text concludes by stating that these main downstream tasks and their corresponding datasets are summarized in Table II.

children.title: B. Evaluation Target
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VI. TASK AND EVALUATION/B. Evaluation Target
children.summary: This section discusses the historical focus of RAG model assessments on specific downstream tasks and the metrics used for them, such as EM, F1, Accuracy, BLEU, and ROUGE. It introduces the main evaluation objectives: Retrieval Quality (measuring context effectiveness) and Generation Quality (assessing the synthesis of coherent answers).

children.title: C. Evaluation Aspects
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VI. TASK AND EVALUATION/C. Evaluation Aspects
children.summary: The section titled 'C. Evaluation Aspects' outlines the primary quality scores and essential abilities used to evaluate RAG models. It details three quality scores: Context Relevance, Answer Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance. Additionally, it describes four required abilities indicative of a model's adaptability and efficiency: Noise Robustness, Negative Rejection, Information Integration, and Counterfactual Robustness.

children.title: D. Evaluation Benchmarks and Tools
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VI. TASK AND EVALUATION/D. Evaluation Benchmarks and Tools
children.summary: This section discusses benchmark tests and tools proposed for evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models. It highlights prominent benchmarks such as RGB, RECALL, and CRUD, which focus on appraising essential RAG abilities. Additionally, it mentions state-of-the-art automated tools like RAGAS, ARES, and TruLens that employ Large Language Models (LLMs) to adjudicate quality scores.

children.title: VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS

children.title: A. RAG vs Long Context
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/A. RAG vs Long Context
children.summary: This section discusses the impact of expanding Large Language Model (LLM) contexts, which now exceed 200,000 tokens. It explores whether Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) remains necessary when LLMs can ingest entire documents directly. The text contrasts RAG with long-context approaches, noting that while long context improves efficiency and allows for complex problem solving, RAG offers benefits like faster inference speed, operational efficiency through chunked retrieval, and verifiable references. The section concludes by identifying the development of new RAG methods for super-long contexts as a future research trend.

children.title: B. RAG Robustness
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/B. RAG Robustness
children.summary: The section 'B. RAG Robustness' discusses the impact of noise or contradictory information on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) output quality, a problem described as 'Misinformation can be worse than no information at all'. It highlights that improving resistance to such adversarial inputs is a key performance metric. The text cites research by Cuconasu et al. [54], which found that including irrelevant documents can unexpectedly increase accuracy by over 30%, contradicting initial assumptions about reduced quality. This underscores the need for specialized strategies to integrate retrieval with language generation models.

children.title: C. Hybrid Approaches
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/C. Hybrid Approaches
children.summary: The section titled 'C. Hybrid Approaches' discusses the emerging strategy of combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with fine-tuning. It highlights the importance of determining the optimal integration method, whether sequential, alternating, or through end-to-end joint training, to effectively harness both parameterized and non-parameterized knowledge.

children.title: D. Scaling laws of RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/D. Scaling laws of RAG
children.summary: This section discusses the scaling laws of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) models. It notes that while scaling laws are established for LLMs, their applicability to RAG remains uncertain. The text highlights that initial studies like RETRO++ have begun addressing this, but parameter counts in RAG models still lag behind those of LLMs. It also mentions the intriguing possibility of an Inverse Scaling Law, where smaller models might outperform larger ones.

children.title: E. Production-Ready RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/E. Production-Ready RAG
children.summary: This section discusses the practicality and engineering requirements of production-ready RAG systems. It highlights key challenges such as enhancing retrieval efficiency, improving document recall in large knowledge bases, and ensuring data security to prevent inadvertent disclosure. The text also notes that the RAG ecosystem is significantly influenced by technical stack advancements, mentioning popular tools like LangChain and LlamaIndex, low-code platforms like Flowise AI, and services from traditional vendors like Weaviate's Verba and Amazon's Kendra. Finally, it identifies a trend towards specialization in RAG technology, focusing on customization and simplification.

children.title: F. Multi-modal RAG
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS/F. Multi-modal RAG
children.summary: Section F discusses the expansion of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) beyond text-based tasks to include multimodal data. It details specific models and methods for handling images, audio, and video. For images, it mentions RA-CM3, BLIP-2, and the 'Visualize Before You Write' method. For audio and video, it describes the GSS method, UEOP, KNN-based attention fusion, Vid2Seq, RBPS, and the CoK method.

children.title: VIII. CONCLUSION
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/VIII. CONCLUSION
children.summary: The conclusion summarizes the paper's emphasis on RAG's advancement in enhancing LLM capabilities by integrating parameterized knowledge with external data. It outlines three developmental paradigms (Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG) and highlights technical integrations like fine-tuning. The section concludes by noting RAG's expanding scope into multimodal domains such as images, videos, and code, underscoring its practical implications for AI deployment.

children.title: REFERENCES
children.path: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey.pdf/Root/REFERENCES
children.summary: This section is a comprehensive bibliography of academic papers and technical reports related to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and large language models. The references cover topics such as retrieval methods, hallucination mitigation, evaluation benchmarks, and specific model architectures. The list includes publications from major conferences like NeurIPS, ACL, EMNLP, and ICSE, as well as arXiv preprints.
